sec.title: Aims
sec.p: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare by enhancing the quality and efficiency of patient care. Nursing students, as future healthcare providers, must be prepared to integrate AI into practice. However, limited research exists on their perceptions and readiness to use AI at King Saud University (KSU) in Saudi Arabia. This study aimed to assess the perceptions and readiness of nursing students toward the use of AI in healthcare and to identify the predictors of their readiness for medical AI.

sec.title: Design
sec.p: A descriptive, cross‐sectional, correlational study was conducted among 304 nursing students selected through convenience sampling.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The General Perceptions of the Use of Artificial Intelligence Applications Scale was used to assess perceptions, while the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (MAIRS‐MS) measured readiness. Data were analysed using appropriate statistical methods.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Overall perception of AI was high (mean = 3.67, SD = 0.91), with the ‘advantages of AI’ scoring the highest (mean = 3.99, SD = 0.81). Readiness for medical AI was also high (mean = 3.79, SD = 0.74). Among the MAIRS‐MS dimensions, ethics scored highest (mean = 3.91, SD = 0.71), followed by ability (mean = 3.86, SD = 0.71), cognition (mean = 3.72, SD = 0.76) and vision (mean = 3.69, SD = 0.78). Predictors of readiness included highest educational attainment (p = 0.007), advantages of AI (p = 0.004) and overall perceptions of AI applications.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare by enhancing diagnosis, treatment, prevention and administrative efficiency. Between 2019 and 2020, the proportion of healthcare organisations utilising AI increased from 55% to 63% (Minor 2021). Major hospitals now use AI systems to support diagnosis, disease prevention and treatment, resulting in more streamlined and effective healthcare provision (Lee and Yoon 2021; Sit et al. 2020). AI applications in medicine include advanced image processing, improved diagnostic accuracy in radiology and pathology, and outcome prediction in patients with atrial fibrillation (Bedi et al. 2023). AI also improves administrative functions such as scheduling, documentation and resource allocation.

Despite these benefits, several challenges hinder AI adoption. Ethical concerns remain prominent, especially regarding patient safety, preferences and privacy (Sit et al. 2020; Chikhaoui et al. 2022). Legal dilemmas also persist, as regulatory frameworks struggle to keep pace with technological advancements (Saeed et al. 2023). In addition, lack of trust, uncertainty about accountability, and liability for AI‐related outcomes may reduce confidence among healthcare professionals (HCPs) (Bajwa et al. 2021).

To ensure effective adoption, HCPs must remain current with technological advances (Demir‐Kaymak et al. 2024). AI enhances both clinical practice and management efficiency, improving overall patient care (Demir‐Kaymak et al. 2024; Martinez‐Ortigosa et al. 2023). Nurses are particularly central to AI integration, serving as end users, educators, leaders and policy advisors (Kwak et al. 2022). AI is reshaping nursing across multiple domains—patient care, policy, administration, education and research. It supports diagnosis through analysis of complex clinical data (Glauberman et al. 2023), improves decision‐making, personalises patient care and enhances operational efficiency (Tang et al. 2024). In research, AI tools strengthen academic writing, accelerate project completion and improve quality (Hwang et al. 2024).

In nursing education, AI‐supported applications and virtual simulations provide immersive learning experiences (Yalcinkaya et al. 2024; Karaca et al. 2021). These tools enhance clinical judgement, digital literacy and research skills (Hwang et al. 2024; Yang 2024). However, concerns about overreliance on technology, algorithmic bias, data privacy and legal liability persist (Pinto dos Santos et al. 2019; Ahmad et al. 2023). Nursing curricula should therefore integrate ethical training, digital literacy and moral sensitivity to prepare students for AI‐enabled healthcare environments (Yang 2024).

Studies assessing nursing students' readiness for AI show mixed findings. Research in Arab nations found moderate knowledge, perception and intention regarding AI use (Al Omari et al. 2024), while a study in Egypt reported poor perceptions among nursing interns (Abdel‐Moaty et al. 2024). In Turkey, nursing students demonstrated moderate readiness, with readiness influencing anxiety levels (Taşkiran 2023), and readiness positively associated with attitudes towards AI (Sumengen et al. 2025). In Saudi Arabia, recent studies reported generally positive perceptions of AI among nursing students (Khodeir et al. 2024; Alsenany et al. 2024), but readiness has not been adequately explored. Given that AI literacy is now viewed as essential for employability, problem‐solving and critical thinking (El‐Sayed et al. 2025), this gap warrants further investigation.

Nursing students also employ AI tools in redaction, removing personal identifiers from medical documents to preserve patient confidentiality while practicing with realistic case data (Alaqra et al. 2018; Nashwan et al. 2023; Makubhai et al. 2023; Pucchio et al. 2022; Schüffler et al. 2021; Rane et al. 2021). This highlights the importance of combining AI literacy with ethical and legal competencies.

Despite increasing global attention, literature on nursing students' perceptions and readiness for AI in Saudi Arabia remains scarce. Therefore, this study aimed to explore perceptions and readiness to utilise AI among nursing students in Saudi Arabia and identify factors influencing their readiness for medical AI.

sec.title: Research Design
sec.p: This study employed a quantitative, descriptive, cross‐sectional, correlational design to assess nursing students' perceptions and readiness to utilise AI at KSU in Saudi Arabia and to identify predictors of readiness.

sec.title: Respondents
sec.p: The study population comprised all nursing students enrolled at KSU in Saudi Arabia between October 18, 2023, and December 16, 2023 (N = 1045). Using an online calculator (Raosoft Inc 2004), the minimum required sample size was determined as 282, based on a 95% confidence level and 5% margin of error. To account for a 20% non‐response rate, 338 students were invited to participate. A convenience sampling method was applied, including undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral nursing students aged 18 years and older, of both genders. Exclusion criteria included students outside the university and those unwilling to participate. Although non‐random, this method was chosen for practicality and ease of access, which may limit the generalisability of findings (Atalla et al. 2024). Ultimately, 304 students completed the survey, yielding an effective response rate of 89.9%.

sec.title: Instruments
sec.p: Perceptions of AI were measured using the General Perceptions of the Use of Artificial Intelligence Applications Scale, which comprises three dimensions—perceptions of AI, advantages of AI and problems associated with AI—across 14 items rated on a five‐point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) (Sumengen et al. 2025). The scale has demonstrated strong reliability in previous studies (α = 0.92) (Atalla et al. 2024; Abdullah and Fakieh 2020). In this study, reliability was acceptable (overall α = 0.714; subscales α = 0.701–0.779). Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported construct validity (KMO = 0.742; Bartlett's test, χ 2 = 1173.677, p < 0.05). All communalities exceeded the recommended 0.60, and the total variance explained was 66.2%, surpassing the acceptable threshold of 60% (Izah et al. 2024; Tabachnick and Fidell 2018; Newlands et al. 2023).

Readiness for AI was assessed using the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (MAIRS‐MS) (Karaca et al. 2021; Alavi et al. 2020). This 22‐item instrument, rated on a five‐point Likert scale, evaluates four dimensions: cognition (8 items), ability (8 items), vision (3 items) and ethics (3 items). Higher mean scores indicate greater readiness. Previous studies have established the reliability and validity of this scale (Sumengen et al. 2025; Alavi et al. 2020). In this study, reliability was excellent (overall α = 0.936; subscales α = 0.843–0.895). CFA confirmed construct validity (KMO = 0.832; Bartlett's test, χ 2 = 5157.505, p < 0.05). All communalities exceeded 0.60, and the total variance explained was 72.1%, above the recommended 60% (Izah et al. 2024; Tabachnick and Fidell 2018; Newlands et al. 2023).

sec.title: Data Collection
sec.p: The survey was administered online via Google Forms. Participants provided informed consent by selecting ‘Agree’ before proceeding; those selecting ‘Disagree’ were exited from the survey. The survey remained open until sufficient responses were obtained, with reminders sent to minimise non‐response bias. Out of 338 invited students, 304 completed the survey. A pilot study with 30 students (October 10–14, 2023) confirmed the clarity, readability and average completion time of approximately 20 min.

sec.title: Ethical Considerations
sec.p: Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB), KSU, Saudi Arabia. The study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Participation was voluntary and without incentives. Students were informed about the study objectives, potential risks and benefits, rights to withdraw at any time, and confidentiality of responses. All data were anonymous, securely stored and accessible only to the research team. Findings were reported in aggregate form, and data were retained in accordance with IRB requirements.

sec.title: Data Analysis
sec.p: Data were exported from Google Forms into IBM SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Descriptive statistics such as frequency, percentage, mean and standard deviation were used to summarise demographic characteristics, perceptions and readiness. Multiple regression analyses were performed to examine the influence of demographic factors and perceptions on readiness for AI. A p‐value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Demographic Profile of Nursing Students
sec.p: The majority of participants were aged 18–40 years (95.1%) and predominantly female (87.8%). Regarding educational level, 45.4% (n = 138) were at the BSN level, 46.1% (n = 140) at the MSN level, and 8.6% (n = 26) at the PhD level. Most students reported a GPA of 4.1 (SD = 0.66), and nearly half (46.1%) had less than one year of clinical experience (Table 1).

sec.title: General Perceptions of AI Applications
sec.p: The overall perception of AI among nursing students was high (mean = 3.67, SD = 0.91). Among the three dimensions, the advantages of AI had the highest mean score (mean = 3.99, SD = 0.81), followed by perceptions of AI (mean = 3.56, SD = 0.96) and AI applications in healthcare (mean = 3.40, SD = 0.96) (Table 2).

sec.p: Within the advantages dimension, the highest‐rated items were ‘AI can improve the practice of healthcare’ (mean = 4.13, SD = 0.75) and ‘AI can offer clinically relevant, high‐quality data’ (mean = 4.03, SD = 0.85). The lowest‐rated item was ‘AI has no space‐time limitation’ (mean = 3.81, SD = 0.87).

In the perceptions dimension, ‘I have hopes about AI applications in healthcare settings’ scored highest (mean = 4.08, SD = 0.74), followed by ‘I have good knowledge of AI’ (mean = 3.63, SD = 0.85). The lowest‐rated item was ‘AI could substitute me in my work’ (mean = 3.13, SD = 1.24).

For the application dimension, the top items were ‘AI has a low capability to empathise and reflect the emotional well‐being of the patient’ (mean = 3.71, SD = 0.97) and ‘AI is not flexible enough to be useful for every patient’ (mean = 3.37, SD = 1.03). The lowest‐rated item was ‘AI is difficult to apply to arguable subjects, such as making definitive patient diagnoses’ (mean = 3.28, SD = 0.92). sec.title: Readiness of Nursing Students for Medical AI
sec.p: Overall readiness for AI was high, with a mean score of 3.79 (SD = 0.74) on the MAIRS‐MS (Table 3, Figure 1).

sec.title: Cognition
sec.p: The highest‐rated items were ‘I can define the basic concepts of statistics’ (mean = 3.97, SD = 0.66), ‘I can properly analyse data obtained by AI in healthcare’ (mean = 3.88, SD = 0.80), and ‘I can define the basic concepts of data science’ (mean = 3.84, SD = 0.64). The lowest rated item was ‘I can explain how AI systems are trained’ (mean = 3.40, SD = 0.94).

sec.title: Ability
sec.p: The highest mean was reported for ‘I find it valuable to use AI for education, service, and research purposes’ (mean = 3.99, SD = 0.75). ‘I can use AI technologies effectively and efficiently in healthcare delivery’ and ‘I can use AI applications in accordance with their purpose’ both scored 3.88 (SD = 0.65).

sec.title: Vision
sec.p: The highest‐rated item was ‘I can explain the strengths and weaknesses of AI technology’ (mean = 3.79, SD = 0.73), and the lowest was ‘I can explain the limitations of AI technology’ (mean = 3.62, SD = 0.82).

sec.title: Ethics
sec.p: ‘I can follow the legal regulations regarding the use of AI technologies in healthcare’ scored highest (mean = 4.00, SD = 0.71), whereas ‘I can act in accordance with ethical principles while using AI technologies’ scored lowest (mean = 3.85, SD = 0.76).

Perceptions of AI and the advantages of using AI were consistent positive predictors across multiple dimensions and overall readiness (p < 0.05) (Table 4).
These findings indicate that both individual demographics and perceptions of AI significantly contribute to nursing students' preparedness to utilise AI in healthcare practice.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study investigated the perception and readiness of nursing students to integrate AI applications into healthcare practice. The findings revealed that participants generally expressed positive perceptions of AI, consistent with recent studies conducted in various contexts (Hammoudi Halat et al. 2024; Petersson et al. 2022; Almalki et al. 2025). Nursing students particularly acknowledged the potential of AI to improve healthcare practice and provide clinically relevant, high‐quality data. This supports earlier research suggesting that AI is increasingly viewed as a promising tool to enhance evidence‐based clinical decision‐making and patient outcomes (Hoelscher and Pugh 2025; Cucci et al. 2025).

However, participants also expressed concerns regarding AI's limitations, including its inability to empathise or adapt flexibly to diverse patient needs. Such findings echo previous reports highlighting that, despite AI's capacity for data analysis and predictive modelling, it cannot substitute the uniquely human aspects of nursing care, such as empathy, ethical judgement and holistic assessment (Rony et al. 2025; Abuadas et al. 2025).

With regard to readiness, students scored moderately high on the MAIRS‐MS scale, indicating a reasonable degree of preparedness to engage with medical AI. They demonstrated confidence in applying AI for education, service and research, as well as in understanding basic data science and statistical concepts. These results align with prior studies reporting similar readiness levels among healthcare students globally (Areshtanab et al. 2025). Nonetheless, gaps were observed in more advanced competencies, such as explaining AI training systems and recognising AI's technical limitations, which suggests the need for targeted education and training (AL‐Olaimat et al. 2025).

The regression analysis offered further insights by demonstrating that demographic and perceptual factors significantly predicted readiness. Specifically, higher educational attainment showed a negative association with certain readiness dimensions, while GPA and perceived advantages of AI were positively correlated. Gender differences were also noted, with female students reporting lower readiness in some areas. These results are in line with earlier literature emphasising the influence of both demographic characteristics and attitudes on healthcare students' acceptance of digital technologies.

Taken together, these findings underscore the need to strengthen nursing curricula by incorporating structured AI education and opportunities for experiential learning. Doing so will help bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application, thereby enabling future nurses to critically evaluate and utilise AI in ways that optimise patient care while upholding ethical and professional standards.

sec.title: Limitations of the Study
sec.p: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study was conducted among a specific population of nursing students, which may limit generalisability to other healthcare disciplines or cultural contexts. Second, the cross‐sectional design restricts the ability to infer causal relationships between demographic characteristics, perceptions, and readiness. Third, the use of self‐reported measures raises the possibility of response bias, as participants may have under‐ or overestimated their competencies. Future research should therefore consider longitudinal designs, include diverse healthcare disciplines, and incorporate objective assessments of AI competence.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study highlighted that nursing students hold positive perceptions of AI and demonstrate moderate readiness to engage with its applications in healthcare. While recognising the advantages of AI, students also noted concerns about its limitations and expressed gaps in advanced technical understanding. Regression analysis revealed that demographic and perceptual variables significantly influenced readiness, highlighting the complex interplay of knowledge, attitudes and context. These findings suggest an urgent need to integrate AI education into nursing curricula and provide students with practical opportunities to develop competence. Such initiatives will better prepare future nurses to engage with AI responsibly and effectively, ensuring its ethical use in improving healthcare delivery.
